claims.text: Controlled heat treatment can maintain or refine the nanoscale precipitate distribution in tungsten-based fusion plasma-facing materials.
Maintaining or refining the nanoscale precipitate distribution reduces high-temperature plastic strain.
Maintaining or refining the nanoscale precipitate distribution enhances fracture toughness.
The proposed improvement in plastic strain and toughness occurs through stabilization or restriction of dislocation motion.
The proposed improvement in plastic strain and toughness occurs through limitation of grain-boundary sliding.
The initial material is a polycrystalline tungsten alloy with a homogeneous distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates at or near grain boundaries act as pinning centers.
A maintained or refined nanoscale precipitate distribution pins dislocations.
A maintained or refined nanoscale precipitate distribution restricts grain-boundary sliding.
Restricting dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding reduces creep deformation.
Restricting dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding improves fracture toughness.
Precipitate coarsening diminishes the proposed pinning effect.
Diminished precipitate pinning permits increased dislocation motion and grain-boundary activity.
Relative to untreated samples, heat-treated samples will exhibit lower creep rates at high temperature.
Relative to untreated samples, heat-treated samples will exhibit greater fracture toughness.
The hypothesized mechanism should apply at approximately 1000–1200 °C when irradiation effects do not dominate.
The hypothesized mechanism should apply to tungsten-based materials having similar compositions and grain sizes.
The magnitude of mechanical improvement may vary with precipitate composition, spacing, and other microstructural parameters.
